---
title: "Let a browser do the clicking"
---

Every test you have written so far talks to a class. It builds a `Bracelet` or a
`WaitingLine` and asks it questions in TypeScript. None of them has ever clicked
a button, so none of them would notice if the Add button in your to-do list
stopped adding anything. This part hands that job to a program that opens a real
browser, types into your page, clicks what a person would click, and reads what
comes back.

The coding buddy for Part 8 knows Playwright, and it is the last one of the
year: nothing in this course is held back from it any more, so it may use every
construct you have learned. Its key replaces the Part 7 key in
`~/.pi/agent/auth.json` (@sec-buddy-setup-new-part).

{{< coding coding-buddy-e2e >}}

## A browser you never see {#sec-playwright-experiment}

1. Create a new app from our tests template. This one carries the experiments of
   the chapter, so it can stay outside `coursework/`.

2. Look inside it. Next to `src/` there is a folder called `e2e/` with one file
   in it, `e2e/add.e2e.ts`, and next to `package.json` there is a
   `playwright.config.ts`. Your `package.json` has a script you have never run:

   ```json
   "test:e2e": "playwright test"
   ```

3. Playwright drives real browsers, and it brings its own copies of them. Fetch
   them:

   ```bash
   npx playwright install
   ```

   This is a big download. Here are the first lines of it, shortened, with the
   progress bar cut down to its last step:

   ```text
   Downloading Chrome for Testing 151.0.7922.34 (playwright chromium v1234)
   |■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■| 100% of 184.3 MiB
   Chrome for Testing 151.0.7922.34 (playwright chromium v1234) downloaded to .../.cache/ms-playwright/chromium-1234
   Downloading Chrome Headless Shell 151.0.7922.34 (playwright chromium-headless-shell v1234)
   |■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■| 100% of 114.7 MiB
   ```

   Firefox and WebKit, the engine behind Safari, follow after those two. Read
   the destination: the browsers land in a cache folder in your home directory,
   not in `node_modules`. You run this command once per computer, not once per
   project, and every app you create from now on finds the browsers already
   there. Your version numbers will be higher than the ones above.

4. Run the test:

   ```bash
   npm run test:e2e
   ```

   ```text
   Running 1 test using 1 worker

     ✓  1 e2e/add.e2e.ts:3:1 › shows the result of adding two numbers (141ms)

     1 passed (1.0s)
   ```

Something started a browser, loaded your app in it, found the line `2 + 3 = 5`
on the page, and closed the browser again, all without a single window appearing
on your screen. That is **headless** mode, and it is the default because it is
faster and because a build server has no screen at all.

Watch it happen once anyway:

```bash
npx playwright test --headed
```

The same test runs, the terminal prints the same summary, and a Chrome window
flashes open in the middle of it. Blink and you miss it, which tells you how
little of your time these tests take.

A test like this is an **end-to-end test**: it uses your app from one end, the
user interface, to the other, the code underneath, exactly the way a person
would.

## What just ran {#sec-playwright-first}

Open `e2e/add.e2e.ts`. There is not much in it:

```ts
import { expect, test } from '@playwright/test';

test('shows the result of adding two numbers', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/');

  await expect(page.getByText('2 + 3 = 5', { exact: true })).toBeVisible();
});
```

The import is the first thing worth noticing. `test` and `expect` come from
`@playwright/test`, not from `'vitest'`. They are different functions with
familiar names, and mixing the two imports in one file is a mistake that
produces confusing errors.

`test('...', callback)` is the shape you know from `it`: a name written as a
sentence, then the callback that holds the test.

The callback is where this file stops looking like a Vitest file. `async
({ page })` says two things at once. The braces around `page` pull one property
out of an object that Playwright passes in, and that property is a fresh, empty
browser tab, made for this one test and thrown away afterwards. Two tests in one
file never see each other's tabs.

The `async` in front of it, and the `await` on every line inside, are there
because your program and the browser are two separate programs. `page.goto('/')`
sends the browser an order and comes straight back with a placeholder for a
result that has not happened yet. That placeholder is called a **promise**, and
`await` means "stop here until the real result arrives". Without it, your test
would fire all its orders in a row and finish before the browser had loaded
anything.

::: {.callout-important}
## The one place this course uses await

`await` belongs in `e2e/*.e2e.ts` and nowhere else in your projects. Every other
file you write this year is ordinary code that runs top to bottom. When your
coding buddy offers you an `async` function in `src/`, say no. MDN has the full
story on promises when you want it.
:::

`page.goto('/')` opens a path, not an address, and the address it hangs the path
on comes from `playwright.config.ts`:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './e2e',
  testMatch: '**/*.e2e.ts',
  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://127.0.0.1:4173',
  },
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run start -- --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4173 --strictPort',
    url: 'http://127.0.0.1:4173',
  },
});
```

`testDir` and `testMatch` say which files are end-to-end tests, which is why
they end in `.e2e.ts` and why Vitest leaves them alone. `baseURL` is the address
`'/'` is measured from. And `webServer` is the part that surprises people:
Playwright runs `npm run start` for you, waits until Vite answers on port 4173,
runs the tests, and shuts the server down again. You never start the app
yourself.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Port 4173 is already used

A run that you stop with Ctrl-C sometimes leaves the Vite server behind, and the
next run refuses to start:

```text
Error: http://127.0.0.1:4173 is already used, make sure that nothing is running
on the port/url or set reuseExistingServer:true in config.webServer.
```

Close that terminal, give the server a few seconds to die, and run again.
:::

The last line reads the page. `getByText('2 + 3 = 5')` on its own would match any
element containing those characters, ignoring upper and lower case, so the
starter adds `{ exact: true }`: the whole text of the element has to be exactly
that. `toBeVisible()` then says what has to be true about it.

## Two kinds of test, two kinds of bug {#sec-playwright-kinds}

Run both test commands in the same app and compare.

```text
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed (1)
   Duration  137ms
```

```text
   1 passed (1.0s)
```

The unit test finishes in a fraction of a second. The end-to-end test needs
about seven times as long for one single assertion, because it starts Vite,
launches a browser, and loads a page before it can check anything.

They are that different because they look at different halves of your app.
`src/math.test.ts` imports `add` and calls it. It never loads `src/index.ts` and
never opens `index.html`, so it cannot notice that you deleted the
`<p id="mathResult">` from the page or misspelled the id in your
`querySelector`. `add` returns 5, the test is green, the app shows nothing.

`e2e/add.e2e.ts` never sees inside `add`. It reads what a visitor reads, which
means it catches the missing paragraph, the misspelled id, the listener you
forgot to register, and the CSS rule that hides the result. What it cannot tell
you is which of those went wrong. It says the text is not on the page, and you
go looking.

You write both kinds, in very different amounts. Rules and arithmetic get many
unit tests, because they are cheap and they name the broken rule exactly. The
paths a user walks get a handful of end-to-end tests, because they are slow and
each one covers a lot of ground.

One rule follows from this, and your coding buddy will hold you to it: an
end-to-end test never imports your app's own modules. The moment a test writes
`import { Bracelet } from '../src/bracelet'`, it has stopped using the app the
way a person does and started being a slow unit test.

## Locators speak the page's language {#sec-playwright-locators}

The starter's page has one paragraph and nothing to click. Give the experiment
app something to drive.

1. Delete `src/math.ts`, `src/math.test.ts`, and `e2e/add.e2e.ts`. You have read
   that test, and its paragraph is about to disappear.

2. Replace the body of `index.html`:

   ```html
   <h1>Greeter</h1>
   <label for="visitorName">Your name</label>
   <input id="visitorName" type="text">
   <button id="greetButton" type="button">Greet me</button>
   <p id="greeting"></p>
   <script src="./src/index.ts" type="module"></script>
   ```

3. Replace `src/index.ts`:

   ```ts
   const visitorName = document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('#visitorName');
   const greetButton = document.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>('#greetButton');
   const greeting = document.querySelector<HTMLParagraphElement>('#greeting');

   if (!visitorName || !greetButton || !greeting) {
     throw new Error('The page is missing one of its elements');
   }

   greetButton.addEventListener('click', () => {
     greeting.textContent = `Hello, ${visitorName.value}!`;
   });
   ```

4. Create `e2e/greeting.e2e.ts`:

   ```ts
   import { expect, test } from '@playwright/test';

   test('greets the visitor by name', async ({ page }) => {
     await page.goto('/');

     await page.getByLabel('Your name').fill('Mia');
     await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Greet me' }).click();

     await expect(page.getByRole('paragraph')).toHaveText('Hello, Mia!');
   });
   ```

5. Run `npm run test:e2e`:

   ```text
   Running 1 test using 1 worker

     ✓  1 e2e/greeting.e2e.ts:3:1 › greets the visitor by name (222ms)

     1 passed (1.2s)
   ```

Everything that starts with `page.getBy...` is a **locator**: a description of an
element, written the way a person would describe it out loud. Read the test
again as a sentence. Fill the field labeled "Your name" with Mia. Click the
button that says "Greet me". The paragraph now has to read "Hello, Mia!".

`getByLabel('Your name')` works because `index.html` carries
`<label for="visitorName">`. That is the rule from @sec-forms-labels, and this is
the payoff it promised: a field with a label is a field your test can name, and a
field without one is a field your test has to hunt for.

`getByRole('button', { name: 'Greet me' })` names two things, the kind of element
and the text a screen reader would announce for it. For a button that text is
simply what is written on it. Roles come from the HTML you chose: a `<button>`
has the role `button` and a `<p>` has the role `paragraph`. The greeter page
holds exactly one paragraph, so `getByRole('paragraph')` needs no name to go
with it.

Then two verbs and two assertions do the work in this chapter:

* `fill(text)` puts text into an input, replacing whatever was in it.
* `click()` clicks the element.
* `toBeVisible()` checks that the element is on the page and can be seen.
* `toHaveText(text)` checks the whole text of the element, character for
  character.

Playwright has a long list of locators and an even longer list of assertions.
Two pages of the [Playwright documentation](https://playwright.dev/docs/intro)
hold both, "Locators" and "Assertions", and you will open them often this part.

## Reading a red run {#sec-playwright-red}

Break the greeter test on purpose. Drop the exclamation mark from the expected
text:

```ts
  await expect(page.getByRole('paragraph')).toHaveText('Hello, Mia');
```

```text
  1) e2e/greeting.e2e.ts:3:1 › greets the visitor by name

    Error: expect(locator).toHaveText(expected) failed

    Locator:  getByRole('paragraph')
    Expected: "Hello, Mia"
    Received: "Hello, Mia!"
    Timeout:  5000ms

    Call log:
      - Expect "toHaveText" with timeout 5000ms
      - waiting for getByRole('paragraph')
        14 × locator resolved to <p id="greeting">Hello, Mia!</p>
           - unexpected value "Hello, Mia!"
```

`Expected` and `Received` read exactly as they do in Vitest, and the element it
found is printed with them, so you can see whether the locator picked the right
thing.

The interesting number is the `14 ×`. A browser is slow in a way a function call
never is: a click starts work that finishes a few milliseconds later, and an
assertion that looked once would sometimes check an element that has not been
filled in yet. So Playwright keeps looking. It checked this paragraph 14 times
over 5 seconds before it gave up. That is why the test above passes in 222
milliseconds and fails in 5 seconds, and it is why no end-to-end test in this
book ever waits for a fixed number of seconds.

Playwright also drops an `error-context.md` into `test-results/` for every
failure, with the error and a description of the page as it saw it. Open it when
a locator finds nothing and you cannot work out why.

Put the exclamation mark back before you go on.

::: {.research title="Three things the exercise needs"}
The three tests you write below check a number of elements, check a class on an
element, and click one of two identical buttons. This chapter does none of the
three, and the [Playwright documentation](https://playwright.dev/docs/intro)
does all of them, on its "Assertions" page and in the "Strictness" part of its
"Locators" page.

1. Which assertion checks how many elements a locator found, so a test can say
   "one item is left in the list" without counting them yourself?
2. Which assertion checks that an element carries a given CSS class?
3. Your page has two buttons that both say `x`. What does Playwright do when a
   locator matches more than one element, and name one way to narrow a locator
   down to the one you want.

For the exam, keep the counting assertion and the answer to the third question
in your head. Almost every list you ever test needs both.
:::

## Exercise: your to-do list under test {#sec-playwright-exercise}

Your to-do list from @sec-creating-elements-exercise was the first app in this
book that built its own elements, and it has never been tested. It is also the
right app to start with, because all of its behavior lives in the page. There is
no class to unit test here, only clicks and what they leave on the screen.

{{< exercise todo-list tests=true >}}

1. Create a new app from our tests template inside `coursework/`, in a folder
   called `todo-e2e`.

2. Delete `src/math.ts`, `src/math.test.ts`, and `e2e/add.e2e.ts`.

3. Copy your own `src/index.ts` from your to-do list project into `src/`. The
   `index.html` and `src/styles.css` you copied in above are the files that
   project started from, so your code will find every element it looks for. This
   step is the point of the exercise: you are testing an app you already wrote,
   not writing a new one.

4. Run `npm start`. Add two items, click one of them to cross it out, and delete
   the other. If that works, the copy is complete. If your project had the open
   count bonus in it, that line keeps working too, and the tests below do not
   care either way.

5. Create `e2e/todo.e2e.ts` and write three tests in it. Every one of them starts
   with `await page.goto('/');` on a fresh, empty list, and every one of them
   uses the New item field and the Add button through their label and their
   text.

   * **shows a new item in the list.** Fill the field with `Buy milk`, click Add,
     and check that `Buy milk` is visible on the page.
   * **crosses an item out when it is clicked.** Add `Buy milk`, then click the
     item itself, and check that the list item now carries the class `done`.
     Your second research answer names the assertion for that.
   * **removes an item when its x button is clicked.** Add `Buy milk` and then
     `Walk the dog`, click the `x` button that belongs to `Buy milk`, and check
     that exactly one list item is left and that it is `Walk the dog`. There are
     two `x` buttons on that page, so read your third research answer before you
     write this one.

6. Run `npm run test:e2e`. Expected result:

   ```text
   Running 3 tests using 1 worker

     ✓  1 e2e/todo.e2e.ts:3:1 › shows a new item in the list (210ms)
     ✓  2 e2e/todo.e2e.ts:12:1 › crosses an item out when it is clicked (166ms)
     ✓  3 e2e/todo.e2e.ts:22:1 › removes an item when its x button is clicked (198ms)

     3 passed (1.6s)
   ```

   Your times will differ. The line numbers will too, unless you wrote the tests
   in the same order and with the same blank lines.

7. Prove that the tests really watch the app. Comment out the line in
   `src/index.ts` that appends the new `li` to the list, run the tests again, and
   read what the three failures say. That run takes about a minute, because a
   click on an element that never appears waits 30 seconds before it gives up.
   Put the line back.

8. Add the `verify` script to `package.json`, with one change:

   ```json
   "verify": "tsc --noEmit && biome check . && vitest run --passWithNoTests"
   ```

   This app has no unit tests, because it has no logic outside the page, and
   `vitest run` treats a project with no test files as a failure:

   ```text
   No test files found, exiting with code 1
   ```

   `--passWithNoTests` turns that into an exit code of 0. Use it here and nowhere
   else: in a project that should have unit tests, the red run is the right
   answer.

9. Run `npm run verify`, fix what it reports, and commit.

Notice what `verify` did not do: it ran TypeScript, Biome, and Vitest, and it
never touched your end-to-end tests. `vitest run` only picks up files ending in
`.test.ts`, so `npm run test:e2e` stays a command of its own. The next chapter
puts both of them into the workflow that runs on every push.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When you finish early

**Test the empty case.** Click Add with an empty field and check that no list
item appears at all. Your Part 2 code already refuses empty text, and this is the
test that says so.

**Test the way back.** Click an item twice and check that the class is gone
again. `classList.toggle` promised both directions; nobody has ever checked the
second one.
:::
